english: Augustine reports that Julian and several fellow bishops sent this letter to Thessalonica. They sought the Eastern bishops’ support “for the catholic faith against Manichaean impiety.” They condemned people who abandon the faith, have a seared conscience, forbid marriage, abstain from foods they consider unclean, and do not believe that everything was created by God (1 Timothy 4:1–4). Their position was that every creature of God is good, and that the supreme God made every substance except God himself, who was not made by anyone.
translator_notes: This is a report of the letter’s opening purpose and teaching, not a continuous surviving quotation. Augustine explicitly says he is passing over some of its appeal to the Eastern bishops. Those omitted portions cannot be recovered from this work.

english: The Roman clergy were so frightened by an order that they were not ashamed to commit the crime of betrayal. In their earlier judgment, their recorded proceedings had supported catholic teaching; afterward, contrary to that judgment, they declared that human nature is evil.
translator_notes: The letter accuses the Roman clergy of reversing their earlier position. Augustine rejects the accusation. The Latin does not identify the issuer of the order in this quoted sentence.

english: In introducing his answer to the letter’s brief accusations, Augustine identifies the disputed claims as these: that Adam’s sin destroyed free will in human nature; that God is not the creator of newborn human beings, or that marriage was instituted by the devil rather than by God; and that what his side calls grace is really fate.
translator_notes: These allegations are recoverable from Augustine’s explicit introduction and denials, not as the letter’s exact surviving words. His positive account of his own teaching is not presented here as part of the letter.

english: Under the name of grace they assert fate: they say that unless God breathes into an unwilling and resisting person a desire for good—even imperfect good—that person can neither turn away from evil nor take hold of good.
translator_notes: The letter is describing and criticizing its opponents’ teaching. Augustine denies that his teaching amounts to fate.

english: We confess that baptism is necessary at every age, and that grace also helps each person’s good purpose, but does not plant the pursuit of virtue in someone who resists, because there is no partiality with God (Colossians 3:25; Romans 2:11).
translator_notes: Augustine quotes this from a later part of the same letter. The source’s Book 2 note identifies Colossians 3:25; its Book 4 note identifies the closer verbal parallel Romans 2:11. Both references are supplied.

english: Augustine says that the authors deny that infants inherit original sin needing remission in baptism. They nevertheless affirm, and indeed proclaim, that the washing of rebirth adopts them from being children of human beings into being children of God (Titus 3:5; John 1:12–13; Romans 8:15).
translator_notes: This is Augustine’s express report of their position, not a verbatim quotation introduced as letter text. The biblical references identify clear language of rebirth and adoption; Augustine’s source has no reference numbers at this sentence. The fuller baptismal statement is preserved at 4.2.2.

english: Augustine attributes this explanation to the authors: “Jacob was loved because of the future works that God knew beforehand he would do” (Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:11–13).
translator_notes: Augustine says “you say” here; he does not expressly identify these words as a verbatim quotation from the letter. The report is retained separately from the letter’s securely quoted passages.

english: Augustine reports that the authors read the saying “It is for a human being to prepare the heart, and the Lord gives the tongue’s answer” as meaning that preparing the heart—that is, beginning something good—belongs to a human being without the help of God’s grace (Proverbs 16:1).
translator_notes: This is Augustine’s account of their interpretation, not an expressly introduced quotation from the letter. His imagined speech beginning “Look, I have prepared my heart without you” is excluded.

english: They say that the law of the Old Testament was not given to justify those who obeyed it, but to become a cause of more serious sin.
translator_notes: Here and in the following accusations, “they” means the letter’s opponents, including Augustine. Augustine replies that this misrepresents him.

english: They also claim that baptism does not truly make people new: that is, that it does not grant full remission of sins. They insist that people become partly children of God but remain partly children of this world—that is, of the devil. (Luke 20:34; possible further echo: 1 John 3:10.)
translator_notes: “Children of this world” clearly recalls Luke 20:34, as Augustine’s immediate reply confirms. “Children of God” and “children of the devil” also have a biblical parallel in 1 John 3:10; this is a possible further allusion. The writers are accusing their opponents, not endorsing this alleged division.

english: They say that “the Holy Spirit was not a helper of virtue under the Old Testament.”
translator_notes: The words inside quotation marks are the allegation preserved by Augustine; “they say that” identifies the opponents whom the letter is accusing. Augustine disputes the allegation. In 3.4.13 he reports the authors’ own distinction: they regard the Spirit as a helper of virtue, while attributing its source to free will rather than to the Spirit.

english: They define all the apostles and prophets as not fully holy, but say that they were less evil by comparison with worse people. They say this is the righteousness to which God bears witness: just as the prophet says that Sodom was justified by comparison with the Jews, so they say that the saints showed some virtue by comparison with criminals (Ezekiel 16:46–52).
translator_notes: This is the letter’s accusation against Augustine’s side. “Justified” here means made to appear righteous by comparison; the decisive comparison is Ezekiel 16:51–52. The source note points more broadly to Ezekiel 16:46 and following.

english: Augustine reports that the letter accused his side of saying that Christ “lied under the compulsion of the flesh.”
translator_notes: Only the words inside quotation marks are preserved here as the accusation’s quoted wording. Augustine denies it and affirms Christ’s freedom from sin. The surrounding discussion of Romans 8:3 and 2 Corinthians 5:21 is Augustine’s explanation, not a scriptural argument quoted from this letter.

english: They say that after the resurrection there will be such progress that people will begin there to fulfill the commandments of God that they were unwilling to fulfill here.
translator_notes: This is an accusation against Augustine’s side. It does not express the authors’ own expectation of the resurrection. Their own statement appears at 4.2.2.

english: They defend the transmission of souls by descent together with the transmission of sin by descent.
translator_notes: The letter accuses Augustine’s side of teaching the propagation of souls as well as inherited sin. Here, unlike passages discussing only the transmission of sin, the Latin explicitly mentions the propagation of souls. Augustine denies having taught this in his writings against the authors.

english: Through Adam, death has passed to us, not wrongdoing (Romans 5:12).
translator_notes: Augustine introduces this as one of the letter’s additional affirmations. The reference identifies the verse under discussion, as his later explanation at 4.4.7 makes explicit.

english: God is the creator of those who are born, and the children of human beings are God’s work. Every sin comes from the will, not from nature.

Baptism is necessary at every age, so that the creature may be adopted among the children of God, not because it inherits anything from its parents that must be cleansed by the washing of rebirth (Titus 3:5; John 1:12–13; Romans 8:15).
translator_notes: Augustine gives this statement in indirect speech. The biblical language of rebirth and divine sonship has been linked; the source prints no reference number at this sentence.

english: They affirm that “the Lord Christ was touched by no stain of sin, as far as his infancy is concerned.”

Augustine reports their explanation as follows: Christ’s flesh was entirely free from the contamination of sin because he shared the nature found in all infants, rather than because of a distinctive excellence and a unique grace.
translator_notes: The first paragraph contains the quoted claim. The second explicitly identifies Augustine’s report of the authors’ explanation; it must not be read as an independently preserved sentence from the letter.

english: Augustine says that the letter raises the question of the soul’s origin and maintains that all infants’ souls, like Christ’s soul, are unstained by sin.
translator_notes: Augustine characterizes the purpose of the letter’s question, but does not quote its wording here. This is retained as a report, not reconstructed as the authors’ verbatim argument.

kind: quotation preserved partly in indirect speech
english: Nothing evil has passed from Adam to everyone else except death (Romans 5:12). Death is not always an evil, since for martyrs it is a cause of rewards. What makes death good or bad is not the dissolution of bodies, which will be raised in every class of human beings (possible echo: John 5:28–29), but the difference in people’s deserts, which arises from human freedom.
translator_notes: The first sentence is given in indirect speech; “they say” introduces the following explanation. The universal resurrection has a possible biblical parallel in John 5:28–29; the source attaches no citation to that clause. The reference to Romans 5:12 is confirmed by Augustine’s discussion at 4.4.7.

kind: quotation preserved partly in indirect speech
english: The Lord says in the Gospel: “He who made them in the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4; Genesis 1:27). And he said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). “Therefore, what God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6).
translator_notes: The letter joins Matthew’s words to Genesis 1:28. Augustine notes that “Increase and multiply” occurs in the law, not in that Gospel passage. The translation preserves the sequence while linking each quotation to its actual location.

english: The old law, which according to the apostle is just, holy, and good, was able to grant everlasting life to those who kept its commandments and lived rightly through faith, as the prophets, patriarchs, and all the saints did (Romans 7:12).
translator_notes: A fuller first-person version is preserved at 4.5.10.

kind: quotation preserved partly in indirect speech
english: Free will has not been lost, since the Lord says through the prophet: “If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land; if you are unwilling and do not listen, the sword will eat you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). Accordingly, grace also helps each person’s good purpose, but does not plant the pursuit of virtue in someone who resists, because there is no partiality with God (Romans 2:11; Colossians 3:25).
translator_notes: The wording “listen to me” and the repeated “eat” preserve the form of Isaiah quoted in the Latin. At 4.6.12 Augustine repeats the last clause as “the sword will consume you.” The grace clause also survives at 2.5.10.

english: Baptism makes people completely new. The apostle is a witness to this, for he testifies that through the washing of water the church gathered from the nations is made holy and spotless (Ephesians 5:26–27).
The Holy Spirit also helped good minds in ancient times, as the prophet says to God: “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path” (Psalm 143:10; LXX Psalm 142:10).
All the prophets, apostles, and saints, both of the New Testament and of the Old, to whom God bears witness, were righteous by the standard of virtue, not by comparison with criminals.

In the time to come there is recompense for good deeds and for bad ones. But no one can fulfill there the commandments that they disregarded here, because the apostle said: “We must appear before Christ’s judgment seat, so that each person may receive what belongs to the body, according to what they have done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10).
translator_notes: The Latin form of Psalm 143:10 says “a straight path”; many modern translations instead have “level ground.” The quotation of 2 Corinthians 5:10 literally says “what belongs to the body”; this compact Old Latin wording is retained, with the sense that people receive recompense for what they did in the body.

english: The good God is the creator of those who are born; through him all things were made, and the children of human beings are his work (John 1:3).
translator_notes: This restatement of the profession includes “through him all things were made,” wording not present in the shorter extract at 4.2.2. The reference identifies its clear biblical allusion.

english: Augustine says that the authors defend Christ’s flesh as “real” and affirm that “the soul itself was touched by no stain of sin.”
translator_notes: Augustine connects the quoted fragments while contrasting their view with the Manichaean claim that Christ’s flesh was absent or only apparent. The passage explicitly affirms the reality of Christ’s flesh and the freedom of his soul from sin; the broader statement about his infancy is preserved at 4.2.2.

english: Augustine reports that in the apostle’s words, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed to all human beings,” the authors understand death, rather than sin, as what passed to everyone (Romans 5:12).
translator_notes: This is Augustine’s express report of the interpretation supporting the letter’s assertion that death, rather than wrongdoing, passed from Adam to his descendants. The scriptural words are quoted by Augustine in stating their interpretation. His following objections concerning “in whom all sinned” are not part of the letter fragment.

english: We acknowledge that the old law too, according to the apostle, is just, holy, and good. It was able to grant everlasting life to those who kept its commandments and lived rightly through faith, as the prophets, patriarchs, and all the saints did (Romans 7:12).
translator_notes: This fuller wording expressly includes “We acknowledge.” The same profession is quoted in indirect form at 4.2.2.

english: All the prophets, apostles, and saints, both those of the Gospel and those of ancient times, to whom God bears witness, were righteous by the standard of virtue, not by comparison with criminals.
In the time to come there is recompense for good deeds and for bad ones, and no one is commanded to fulfill there the commandments that they disregarded here.
translator_notes: Augustine interrupts the letter’s wording with statements of agreement. These have been removed, while the two claims he quotes are retained. The second paragraph has “no one is commanded” here, whereas 4.2.2 has “no one can”; both forms are preserved. The Holy Spirit clause repeated here is already given in full at 4.2.2.

english: Their enemies have adopted Augustine’s statements out of hatred for the truth. Throughout the entire West, a doctrine as foolish as it is impious has been accepted. Signatures confirming it have been extorted from unsuspecting bishops who remained in their own places, without a synod being assembled.
translator_notes: Augustine gives the complaint in indirect speech and calls the adopted statements “our statements.” The translation identifies him rather than misleadingly making “our” refer to the letter’s authors. “Unsuspecting” renders simplicibus, which can also mean simple or unsophisticated. The complaint about the Western reception is repeated at 4.12.33; the complaint about signatures is directly quoted at 4.12.34.
